You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: The best financial report in AMD’s history leads to a 9% plunge: the market wants acceleration, not just good results

TEXT:
After market close on August 4, AMD delivered an almost flawless earnings report: revenue reached $11.536 billion, up 50% year-over-year, setting a record high; non-GAAP EPS was $1.66, surpassing the market expectation of $1.62; data center revenue hit $6.718 billion, doubling year-over-year and accounting for 58% of total company revenue. However, in after-hours trading, AMD's stock price once plunged 10% and closed down 8.8%.
Why did results that beat expectations turn out to be a negative? What the market prices in is not performance, but acceleration. AMD’s share price has surged over 130% this year, with a 52-week range from $149 to $584, driven by expectations of “catching up to Nvidia.” Q3 guidance is around $13 billion, higher than the consensus of $12.5 billion, but quarter-on-quarter growth is only 13%—maintaining the slope, not taking a leap. The market wanted acceleration, but the earnings report didn’t deliver it.
The cost of investing is also reflected in the report: Gross margin hit a new high at 56%, but AI data center’s gross margin is below the company average, and the growth segment comprising 58% of revenue is actually diluting company margins; to secure capacity for Helios cabinet systems, capital expenditure reached $808 million, nearly three times analysts’ expectations, slashing free cash flow from $2.57 billion to $1.56 billion. The cost of growth is now clearly visible on the balance sheet for the first time.
The acceleration the market wants: Q3 guidance didn't deliver
Q3 guidance of about $13 billion represents a 41% YoY increase and 13% QoQ growth, with the midpoint above consensus of $12.52 billion. The guidance isn't bad per se, the issue is with its shape: quarter-on-quarter growth is only 13%, just maintaining the current slope.
Dolphin Research did the math: Based on guidance, the quarter-on-quarter increment for data center is about $1.2 to $1.8 billion, but the MI455X has just started shipping, so the step up isn't particularly strong. The market previously bet that AI demand would allow AMD to take another leap forward, but the guidance didn't send that signal.
AMD’s 130% gain this year is built on a narrative: Nvidia’s capacity is constrained, clients need a second supplier, and AMD is shifting from an AI chip alternative to a must-have. The mission of this earnings report was to prove the acceleration of this story.
In July, Anthropic announced deployment of 2GW MI450 GPUs on Helios, sending AMD’s stock up about 10% on the day; in early June, Broadcom’s earnings triggered a semiconductor sector pullback, after which AMD rebounded above $518 on expectations for Helios orders. Each rally raises the bar for the next earnings report.
When all AMD delivers is "as-expected outperformance," there's no reason for the 130% rally to continue. The after-hours selling was the realization of these expectations.
107% YoY doubling—half of it comes from a low base
The 107% YoY growth in data center revenue is eye-catching but needs context.
In Q2 2025, U.S. export controls led AMD to write down $800 million in MI308 inventory and related charges, creating an artificially low base. This year’s doubling is in part just climbing out of that hole.
Dolphin Research broke down the numbers: This quarter, Instinct AI GPU revenue was about $2.7 billion, versus $1.1 billion a year ago, again influenced by the low base. In contrast, EPYC is “cleaner”: cloud and enterprise sales both grew over 70% YoY, server CPU revenue hit records for a fifth consecutive quarter, and the sixth-generation EPYC Venice is in production. Acceleration without low-base distortion is the most solid aspect of this earnings report.
Lisa Su gave an anchor on the earnings call: data center revenue will "more than double" by 2027, with server revenue expected to grow over 80% YoY in the second half of 2026, and continue growing more than 70% in 2027 off a higher base.
The underlying story of gross margin: The bigger AI gets, the slimmer the margin
The 56% non-GAAP gross margin is a new high, but the number has distortions. Over half of the 13 percentage point YoY jump comes from last year’s $800 million export control writedown.
Management confirmed on the call: The gross margin of AI data centers is slightly below the company average. And data centers are both the fastest-growing and the largest business, rising from 42% of revenue a year ago to 58% now. The fastest-growing part of the business structurally dilutes margin.
By comparison, Nvidia’s non-GAAP gross margin is 75%, a gap of nearly 20 points. Nvidia leverages monopoly pricing for excess profits, while AMD gains market share by competing on price—Lisa Su put it plainly: AMD sells end-to-end infrastructure integrating CPU, GPU, and network chips, using lower pricing and greater openness to attract clients. The consequence is a naturally lower profit ratio for every dollar of revenue compared to the competition.
[...]
This is AMD's first full-rack AI system, delivering CPUs, GPUs, and network chips packaged as a complete cabinet—first shipments went to Meta, OpenAI, and Oracle this quarter; the July-announced Anthropic 2GW collaboration has its first gigawatt deployment beginning in the first half of 2027; Microsoft will also deploy at scale in Azure. The client list continues to expand: Anthropic, Cirrascale, HUMAIN, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, Tensorwave, Vultr.
[...]
HSBC downgraded AMD to Hold in May, specifically citing TSMC capacity limits—this earnings report, to an extent, confirms that concern, otherwise AMD wouldn’t need to take capital expenditures to three times estimates to secure capacity. The AI chip competition is no longer about whose chip is better, but who can secure TSMC capacity first. Nvidia’s priority remains an unavoidable constraint for AMD.
[...]
Helios also suggests a deeper shift: AMD’s business model is moving from selling chips to selling systems. Previously, they sold GPUs and CPUs by the piece, and customers built their own clusters; now, they deliver full cabinets, which are more expensive and complex to fulfill. This is both an attack and a defense—Nvidia has long proven that system-level products mean higher margins and customer stickiness than single chips. But the shift also means heavier capital and greater fulfillment risk: if a cabinet fails, AMD’s role shifts from chipmaker to system integrator.
[...]
Nvidia holds about 80% share in the AI accelerator market, AMD around 10–15%; Nvidia’s single-quarter data center revenue is $75.2 billion, 11 times AMD’s total data center business. Still, after surging 130% this year, AMD’s forward P/E is now significantly higher than Nvidia’s—and analysts are split: Morgan Stanley questions valuation, while Benchmark offers a $685 price target.
[...]
Nvidia is the next test
[...]
Then, keep an eye on Nvidia. Its next earnings are due August 26; last quarter, its data center revenue was $75.2 billion, up 92% YoY. Even AMD’s comprehensive beat couldn’t drive the stock higher—how high is the expectation bar for Nvidia now? When beating expectations becomes the baseline, and only massive outperformance can move the stock, every AI chip earnings season turns into a harder and harder exam.
[...]
In the next month, the market will be focused on three things: whether AMD's stock holds $470, whether Nvidia's August 26 results meet the higher bar, and whether TSMC's capacity allocation tilts toward AMD. Further out, three hard metrics will validate the “doubling guidance”: the initial 1 GW Anthropic deployment in H1 2027, the quarterly ramp of MI455X shipments, and whether AI data center margins improve with scale. The AI chip arms race is far from over—it’s just moved from telling stories to delivering results.
